newsitem.title: USA: NYS lawmakers seen agreeing on surplus, not budget.
newsitem.headline: NYS lawmakers seen agreeing on surplus, not budget.

text.p: New York State lawmakers expect Albany to have as much as $2.8 billion more than first estimated in fiscal 1998, financial sources said Monday.
But lawmakers still cannot agree on a new budget, which was due April 1.
"I think we would not be near the ninth inning if this was a baseball game. Absent a rain delay, we still have a ways to go," Gov George Pataki told reporters in Albany.

A number of issues were delaying progress, most recently a fight over how about $350 million would be spent under a $1.75 billion green bond that voters approved last November to pay for cleaning up the state's air, water and industrial sites.
"The environmental bond act, we're not going to allow become a patronage tool for politicians," Pataki said, adding spending must be based on objective criteria that were the most cost-effective.
Later, he added: "I'm not looking to tar anybody," and the Republican governor did not disclose what specific spending proposals he objected to.

Pataki proposed a bill to give the public a say in selecting projects funded by the green bond. Review committees with environmental and public health experts, as well as labor, business, agency and legislative representatives would be created to make comments before a final list of projects was established.

The three-way, leaders' talks were expected to resume as soon as late Monday, but Albany looked likely to break the new, national record it set last year when it failed to produce a new budget until July 13.

A fight over building more prisons also was a key obstacle in Pataki's eyes.The governor has proposed selling $650 million of revenue bonds to pay for new prisons, a plan attacked as too costly and as unconstitutional by state Assemblyman Daniel Feldman, D-Brooklyn, and the League of Women Voters for New York State.
The issue is an important one for Pataki, as job-hungry, upstate communities, which tend to be Republican strongholds, are expected to ask that any new prisons be built in their areas.

Pataki said his talks with the Assembly Speaker, Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, and the Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, focused on how much prison capacity was needed. The Assembly has projected a lower prison population than the governor.
Silver, the Assembly Speaker, said a comprehensive program was needed, and his stand appeared to put him at least partly at loggerheads with the governor.

"It doesn't use prisons as an economic development tool, although it does use prisons as way to help local governments that have excess capacity," he said, referring to his program, which included spending on police officers through-out the state, cheaper beds as part of an anti-drug program and more shelter beds.
Asked if he still refused to go along with building more prisons, Silver replied: "Without being specific as to the details of the discussion, we think that discussion has a broad approach to it."

Modifying the welfare system was another big hang-up, with Pataki, who wants tougher changes than the Assembly, saying agreement was needed as counties and cities cannot comply with new federal rules until Albany approved a new state plan.

Despite the differences highlighted by the governor, Senate Majority Leader Bruno said some progress had been made, and attempted to defuse tensions seen on Sunday, when his Democratic counterpart arrived late for a meeting. Asked why things had improved since then, Bruno said:

"Well, because I think we've had a rather direct and specific discussion on what's inhibiting our ability to go forward, and you know, when you get some clarity on what's keeping you from going forward, then you can try and work on getting there." He added issues like energy, education, taxes and school choice also remain outstanding.
Silver focused on battles over education, higher education and healthcare, and economic development, saying they were priorities.
